entry_json.definition: not including someone or something

I like all kinds of music except heavy metal.

entry_json.definition: feeling very happy because something good is going to happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was excited about moving abroad, though I was nervous too.

I am excited about starting the new course.

entry_json.definition: making you feel happy and interested; full of things that happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Moving to a new city was the most exciting year of my life.

The job offers exciting opportunities to travel.

entry_json.definition: activity that you do to keep your body strong and healthy; also a task for practice
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get most of my exercise by cycling to work.
example_sentences: Regular exercise reduces the risk of heart disease.
Do the grammar exercises on page forty.

entry_json.definition: to be real, or to be present in the world
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The problem existed long before anyone wrote about it.

No such rule exists here.

entry_json.definition: to think that something will probably happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I expect the results to arrive within two weeks.

Employers expect graduates to have some work experience.

entry_json.definition: costing a lot of money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Renting in the city centre is far too expensive for most students.
example_sentences: Organic food is expensive but better for the soil.
It was the most expensive mistake of my career.

confusables.difference: Things are expensive; prices and costs are high. Say "an expensive flat" but "a high price", never "an expensive price".

entry_json.definition: the knowledge and skill you get from doing something; also an event that affects you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Two years of teaching gave me more experience than any course could.
example_sentences: The job requires at least three years' experience.
Living abroad was a difficult but valuable experience.
entry_json.avoid: Uncountable when it means knowledge (much experience), countable when it means an event (a strange experience). Not "many experiences" for skill.

entry_json.definition: a careful test done to find out if an idea is true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: In the experiment, one group slept eight hours and the other only five.
example_sentences: The experiment was repeated three times.
Animal experiments remain controversial.

entry_json.definition: a person who knows a great deal about a particular subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Health experts agree that walking is the easiest exercise to keep up.
example_sentences: She is an expert on renewable energy.
You do not need to be an expert to use the software.
entry_json.avoid: An expert is expert ON or IN a subject, not "expert about".

entry_json.definition: to tell someone about something in a way that makes it easy to understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My teacher explained the difference to me twice before I understood it.
example_sentences: Can you explain how the system works?
The report explains why the costs rose.
entry_json.avoid: Never "explain me". You explain something TO someone: "explain it to me".

entry_json.definition: a statement that makes something clear or easy to understand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a simple explanation for the drop in visitor numbers.
example_sentences: He offered no explanation for being late.
The book gives a clear explanation of the theory.

entry_json.definition: to say or show what you think or feel
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me a year to express my ideas in English without hesitating.
example_sentences: Several residents expressed concern about the new road.
She finds it hard to express her feelings.

entry_json.definition: a word or phrase used in a particular way; also the look on your face
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a notebook of useful expressions for the speaking test.
example_sentences: "To cut a long story short" is a common English expression.
There was a worried expression on his face.

entry_json.definition: more than the usual or expected amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I took an extra hour each evening to review what I had learned.
example_sentences: There is an extra charge for luggage.
Staff were paid extra for working weekends.

entry_json.definition: very great in degree; much more than normal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Extreme weather is becoming more common in parts of the country.
example_sentences: The desert has extreme temperatures at night.
Some of the views expressed were quite extreme.

entry_json.definition: to a very great degree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Finding a flat near the university was extremely difficult.
example_sentences: The test was extremely well organised.
Water is extremely scarce in that region.
entry_json.avoid: Extremely goes with normal adjectives (extremely cold), not with extreme ones. Not "extremely enormous".

entry_json.definition: one of the two parts of the body that you see with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Staring at a screen all day leaves my eyes tired.
example_sentences: She has dark brown eyes.
Close your eyes for a moment and rest.

entry_json.definition: the front part of your head, where your eyes and mouth are
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You could see from her face that the news was good.
example_sentences: Wash your face in cold water to wake up.
I never forget a face, but I always forget names.

entry_json.definition: a thing that is known to be true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fact that so few people vote should worry the government.
example_sentences: Check your facts before you write the essay.
In fact, the opposite happened.

entry_json.definition: one of the things that helps to cause a result
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Cost is the main factor stopping people from cycling to work.
example_sentences: Several factors explain the fall in sales.
Diet is an important factor in heart disease.

entry_json.definition: a building where things are made in large numbers by machines
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The car factory closed and two thousand people lost their jobs.
example_sentences: Most of the clothes are made in factories overseas.
The factory runs twenty-four hours a day.

entry_json.definition: to not succeed in something you are trying to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I failed my first driving test because I was too nervous.
example_sentences: The plan failed for a simple reason: nobody explained it.
Students who fail the exam can retake it in June.

confusables.difference: You fail a test you took and did badly in. You miss a class or a bus you did not get to at all.

entry_json.definition: right and the same for everyone; not helping one person more than another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is not fair that some students pay far more for the same degree.
example_sentences: The referee's decision seemed fair to both sides.
Workers are asking for a fair wage.

entry_json.definition: to move down towards the ground; also to become lower in number or level
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unemployment fell steadily between 2015 and 2019.
example_sentences: Be careful on the steps; the ice makes people fall.
House prices fell sharply after the crisis.
entry_json.avoid: Fall is irregular: fall, fell, fallen. "Prices falled" is always wrong.

entry_json.definition: not true or not correct
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Decide whether each statement is true or false.
example_sentences: The article contained several false claims.
He gave a false name at the hotel.

entry_json.definition: a group of people who belong together, such as parents and children
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I come from a large family, so the house was never quiet.
example_sentences: My family live in a small town in the north.
Family size has fallen in most developed countries.

entry_json.definition: known about by very many people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city is famous for its old bridges and its food.
example_sentences: She is a famous scientist in her field.
It is one of the most famous buildings in the world.
entry_json.avoid: Famous FOR a thing, famous AS a role: "famous for its cheese", "famous as a writer".

entry_json.definition: a person who likes a sport, singer or team very much; also a machine that moves air
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have been a fan of that team since I was a child.
example_sentences: Thousands of fans waited outside the stadium.
The office fan is the only thing keeping us cool.

entry_json.definition: extremely good
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The food at the festival was fantastic and surprisingly cheap.
example_sentences: We had a fantastic time in the mountains.
That is a fantastic idea.
entry_json.avoid: Fantastic is informal. In Task 2 writing, prefer "excellent" or "highly effective".

entry_json.definition: a long way from a place
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The nearest hospital is quite far from the village.
example_sentences: How far is the station from here?
Rents are far higher than they were five years ago.
entry_json.avoid: In positive statements we usually say "a long way", not "far": "It is a long way from here." Far is natural in questions and negatives.

entry_json.definition: an area of land where people grow food or keep animals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandparents ran a small farm and grew most of what they ate.
example_sentences: The farm has been in the family for a century.
Wind farms now cover part of the hillside.

entry_json.definition: a person who owns or works on a farm
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farmers in the region depend on one rainy season each year.
example_sentences: My uncle is a rice farmer.
Farmers are being paid to plant trees.

entry_json.definition: the work of growing food on land, or keeping animals
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Farming employs fewer people than it did, but it still feeds us all.
example_sentences: Organic farming uses fewer chemicals.
Farming methods have changed enormously since 1950.

entry_json.definition: the style of clothes that is popular at a particular time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fast fashion is cheap for the shopper and expensive for the planet.
example_sentences: Long coats are back in fashion this winter.
She works in the fashion industry.

entry_json.definition: moving or happening at high speed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A fast train would cut the journey from four hours to two.
example_sentences: The internet connection here is not very fast.
She is a fast reader.

confusables.difference: Fast usually describes movement (a fast car). Quick usually describes a short time (a quick meeting). Both can mean speedy.
Fast is both adjective and adverb: "he runs fast". There is no word "fastly".

entry_json.definition: having too much flesh on the body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Doctors avoid the word fat and say overweight instead.
example_sentences: The dog has got fat because nobody walks it.
Fatty foods should be eaten in small amounts.
entry_json.avoid: Calling a person fat is rude in English. Use "overweight" when writing or speaking politely.

entry_json.definition: a man who has a child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My father taught me to cook before I left home.
example_sentences: He became a father at twenty-five.
Fathers now take more time off work than they used to.

entry_json.definition: liked more than all the others
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My favourite time of day is early morning, before anyone else is up.
example_sentences: What is your favourite subject at school?
This is my favourite café in the whole city.
entry_json.avoid: Favourite is already the top choice, so "most favourite" is wrong. British spelling keeps the u: favourite.

entry_json.definition: the bad feeling you have when you think something dangerous may happen
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fear of speaking in public stopped me applying for the job for years.
example_sentences: Many people have a fear of flying.
There are fears that prices will rise again.

entry_json.definition: an important or noticeable part of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The main feature of the new library is that it never closes.
example_sentences: The app has several useful features.
Heavy rainfall is a feature of the region's climate.

entry_json.definition: to give food to a person or animal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme feeds around two hundred children every school day.
example_sentences: I feed the cat before I leave for work.
The country can no longer feed itself without imports.

entry_json.definition: to know something in your body or your mind, for example when you are happy, tired or cold
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I felt much calmer once I had practised the test under real conditions.
example_sentences: Do you feel tired in the afternoon?
Many workers feel that they are not listened to.
entry_json.avoid: After feel, use an adjective, not an adverb: "I feel bad", not "I feel badly".

entry_json.definition: what you feel in your mind or body, for example when you are happy, sad or worried
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had a feeling that the interview had gone badly, and I was right.
example_sentences: It is not always easy to describe your feelings.
There were mixed feelings about the decision.

entry_json.definition: being a woman or a girl; in animals, being the one that can have babies or eggs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only a quarter of the engineering students were female.
example_sentences: The chart compares male and female employment rates.
Female doctors outnumber male doctors in some countries.

confusables.difference: Female is the technical or statistical word, used with nouns: female students. Woman is the ordinary word for a person: "a woman I know".

entry_json.definition: a special time when people celebrate something, often with music or food
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The rice festival at home lasts three days and everyone stops working.
example_sentences: The city holds a film festival every autumn.
Music festivals bring thousands of visitors.

entry_json.definition: stories about people and events that are not real
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I read fiction on the train and non-fiction at my desk.
example_sentences: The novel is a work of science fiction.
Children who read fiction develop wider vocabulary.

entry_json.definition: an area of land used for growing food or playing sport; also a subject you work or study in
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She is one of the leading researchers in her field.
example_sentences: The children were playing football in the field behind the school.
Farmers plant these fields with wheat every spring.
collocations: a leading figure in the field

entry_json.definition: to hit or attack someone; also to try hard to stop something bad
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Governments must fight air pollution, not just measure it.
example_sentences: The two boys were fighting in the playground.
She has spent years fighting for equal pay.

entry_json.definition: a number, especially one in a report or a chart
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The figures show a steady rise in car ownership since 2000.
example_sentences: Unemployment figures are published every month.
Sales reached a record figure last year.
entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, "the figure" can mean the chart itself or a number. Say "the chart shows" to stay clear.

entry_json.definition: to make something full, or to put information in the spaces on a form
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fill in the application form and bring it to the office in person.
example_sentences: Please fill the bottle before you leave.
The hall filled quickly once the doors opened.

confusables.difference: Fill means make full. Feel is about emotion or touch. They are spelled and pronounced differently: fill has a short i, feel a long ee.

entry_json.definition: a story told in moving pictures, shown at the cinema or on television
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We watch one film in English every weekend with the subtitles off.
example_sentences: The film is based on a true story.
British speakers say film; Americans usually say movie.

entry_json.definition: last, coming at the end
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The final section of the reading test is always the hardest.
example_sentences: The final decision rests with the manager.
In the final paragraph, restate your opinion.

entry_json.own_context_sentence: Finally, I would argue that education matters more than income.
example_sentences: The bus finally arrived forty minutes late.
Finally, I would like to thank my supervisor.

confusables.difference: Finally can simply mark your last point in an essay. "At last" always carries relief that a long wait is over.

entry_json.definition: to discover where something or someone is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It took me three weeks to find a flat I could afford.
example_sentences: I cannot find my student card anywhere.
Researchers found that sleep improved test scores.
entry_json.avoid: Find is irregular: find, found, found. "Finded" does not exist.

entry_json.definition: good enough; healthy and well

Tuesday at three is fine for me.
entry_json.avoid: "Fine" as an answer is informal and vague. In Speaking Part 1, add a reason rather than stopping at "fine".

entry_json.definition: one of the five long parts at the end of your hand
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cut my finger while chopping vegetables and could not write for days.
example_sentences: He pointed a finger at the map.
She wears a ring on her middle finger.

entry_json.definition: to come to the end of something, or to complete it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I finished writing the essay an hour before the deadline.
example_sentences: The lecture finishes at four.
Have you finished your homework?
entry_json.avoid: Finish is followed by -ing, not to: "I finished reading", never "I finished to read".

entry_json.definition: the hot, bright light you see when something burns
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A fire in the market destroyed twenty small shops overnight.
example_sentences: The fire was put out within an hour.
Forest fires are becoming more frequent.

entry_json.own_context_sentence: Firstly, city centres should be closed to private cars.
example_sentences: Firstly, the cost is far too high.
Firstly, I will describe the process; secondly, I will explain it.

confusables.difference: Firstly introduces your first point in an argument. "At first" describes how something was at the start but later changed: at first I hated it.

entry_json.definition: an animal that lives in water and swims, often eaten as food
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We eat fish twice a week because the coast is only an hour away.
example_sentences: Fish stocks in the North Sea have fallen sharply.
I bought some fresh fish at the market.
entry_json.avoid: The plural is usually "fish", not "fishes": "I caught three fish".

entry_json.definition: the activity or business of catching fish
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fishing was the main industry here before the tourists came.
example_sentences: He goes fishing every Sunday morning.
Overfishing has damaged the fishing industry itself.

entry_json.own_context_sentence: The jacket does not fit me any more, but I keep it anyway.
example_sentences: These shoes fit perfectly.
The desk will not fit in that corner.

confusables.difference: Fit is about size. Suit is about whether something looks right on you or is convenient. A shirt can fit you but not suit you.

entry_json.definition: to repair something that is broken; also to decide a date or price
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The landlord took two months to fix the heating.

entry_json.definition: a set of rooms for living in, usually on one floor of a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I share a two-bedroom flat with a colleague to keep the rent down.
example_sentences: The flat is on the fourth floor with no lift.
Flats near the station are the most expensive.

confusables.difference: Flat is the British word and apartment the American one. IELTS accepts both, but stay consistent within one answer.

entry_json.definition: a journey made by air
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flight was delayed by three hours because of the weather.
example_sentences: I booked a cheap flight to Rome.
Short domestic flights produce a lot of carbon.

entry_json.definition: the part of a room that you walk on; also one level of a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Our office is on the third floor and the lift is always broken.
example_sentences: The children sat on the floor.
The building has twelve floors.
entry_json.avoid: In Britain, the floor at street level is the ground floor, and the one above it is the first floor.

entry_json.definition: the part of a plant that has bright colours and often a sweet smell
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My mother grows flowers on the balcony of a very small flat.
example_sentences: I bought her flowers for her birthday.
The park is full of spring flowers in April.

entry_json.definition: an illness like a bad cold, with a high temperature and pain in your body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had flu during the exam period and had to postpone one paper.
example_sentences: Half the office is off with flu.
Older people are offered a flu vaccine every autumn.

entry_json.definition: to move through the air; also to travel by plane
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I fly home once a year, and the ticket takes months to save for.
example_sentences: Birds fly south before the winter.
It is cheaper to fly than to take the train on that route.
entry_json.avoid: Fly is irregular: fly, flew, flown.

entry_json.definition: travelling by plane
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Flying is fast, but it is by far the most damaging way to travel.
example_sentences: He has a real fear of flying.
Flying short distances should be taxed more heavily.

entry_json.definition: to give all your attention to one thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: For the last month I focused only on writing and left reading aside.
example_sentences: The report focuses on rural schools.

entry_json.avoid: Focus takes ON: "focus on the problem", not "focus to the problem".

entry_json.definition: to go after someone or something; also to do what a rule or instruction says
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Follow the signs to the exam hall rather than asking at reception.

If you follow these steps, the process is simple.

entry_json.definition: coming next, or listed below
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The following table shows the results for each age group.
example_sentences: We met on the Friday and he left the following morning.

confusables.difference: "The following day" looks forward from a past point in a story. "Next" is usually counted from now: next Monday.

entry_json.definition: the things that people and animals eat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Food prices have risen faster than wages in the last two years.
example_sentences: Street food is cheap and often better than restaurant food.
The charity provides food for families in need.
entry_json.avoid: Food is uncountable in general use: "a lot of food", not "many foods", unless you mean different types.

entry_json.definition: the part of the body at the end of the leg that you stand on
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I walk to work on foot, which takes twenty-five minutes.

The village is at the foot of a hill.
entry_json.avoid: The plural is feet, not foots. "On foot" is always singular.

entry_json.definition: a game in which two teams try to get a ball into a goal with their feet
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Football is the one thing everyone in my family agrees about.
example_sentences: We play football in the park on Sundays.
Football clubs earn huge sums from television.
entry_json.avoid: We play football with no article: "play football", not "play the football".

entry_json.definition: used to show who gets something, why you do it, or how long it lasts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in this city for six years and still find new streets.
example_sentences: This letter is for you.
She worked for the same company for a decade.

confusables.difference: For gives a length of time: for three years. Since gives a starting point: since 2019. "For 2019" is always wrong.

entry_json.definition: belonging to or coming from a country that is not your own
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a foreign language opened more doors than my degree did.
example_sentences: The university attracts foreign students from sixty countries.
Foreign investment has grown steadily.
entry_json.avoid: Do not use foreign about a person to their face; it can sound cold. Say "international students" in writing.

entry_json.definition: a large area of land covered with trees
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The forest behind our village has shrunk by half in thirty years.
example_sentences: Rainforests absorb huge amounts of carbon.
Forest fires destroyed thousands of hectares.

entry_json.definition: to fail to remember something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I always forget names, so I write them down immediately.
example_sentences: Do not forget to bring your passport.
I will never forget the day the results came out.

confusables.difference: You forget a fact, but you leave an object in a place: "I left my umbrella on the bus", not "I forgot my umbrella on the bus".

entry_json.definition: a tool with points at the end, used for picking up food
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I still eat rice with my hands at home and with a fork elsewhere.
example_sentences: Put the knives and forks on the table.
He ate the salad with a small fork.

entry_json.definition: a paper with spaces where you write your name and other information; also a type of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I filled in the visa form three times before it was accepted.
example_sentences: Complete the form in black ink.
Cycling is the cheapest form of transport in a busy city.

entry_json.definition: using the polite, careful language and behaviour of serious or important times and places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Task 2 needs formal English, so I avoid contractions and slang.
example_sentences: The letter should be written in formal language.
It was a formal dinner, so we all wore suits.

confusables.difference: Formal is for essays, official letters and strangers. Informal is for friends and everyday speech. IELTS Writing Task 2 must be formal; Speaking may be neutral.

entry_json.definition: luckily; used when something good happens
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fortunately, the library stayed open late during the exam period.
example_sentences: Fortunately, nobody was hurt in the accident.
Fortunately, the flight was only slightly delayed.

confusables.difference: Fortunately introduces good news; unfortunately introduces bad news. Both go at the start of the sentence with a comma.

entry_json.definition: towards a place or position in front
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The queue moved forward slowly in the rain.
example_sentences: He stepped forward to answer the question.
I look forward to hearing from you.
entry_json.avoid: "Look forward to" is followed by -ing: "I look forward to meeting you", not "to meet you".

entry_json.definition: costing no money; or not busy, or not controlled by anyone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Museum entry is free here, which is why I go so often.

Free healthcare is paid for through taxation.

entry_json.definition: recently made, picked or grown; not old and not kept for a long time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Fresh vegetables cost more in winter, so we buy frozen ones.
example_sentences: I opened the window to get some fresh air.
The bread is baked fresh every morning.

entry_json.definition: a cold cupboard that keeps food from going bad
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was nothing in the fridge except milk and half a lemon.
example_sentences: Put the fish in the fridge straight away.

entry_json.definition: a person you like and enjoy spending time with
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Most of my closest friends are people I met in my first year of university.
example_sentences: I am meeting a friend for coffee later.
She made friends easily in the new city.
entry_json.avoid: We say "make friends", never "do friends" or "find friends".

entry_json.definition: kind and nice to other people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The people in my neighbourhood are friendly, which made moving easier.
example_sentences: The staff at the hostel were very friendly.

entry_json.definition: something you enjoy doing in your free time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Photography started as a hobby and slowly turned into work.
example_sentences: My main hobby is cooking.
Hobbies help people switch off after work.
entry_json.avoid: The plural is hobbies. In Speaking Part 1, name one hobby and give a reason rather than listing three.

entry_json.definition: a game played by two teams who hit a small ball with long sticks
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Hockey is the one sport my old school was actually good at.
example_sentences: She played hockey for the county.
Hockey matches are played on artificial grass.

entry_json.definition: to keep something in your hand; also to organise an event
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The conference is held in a different city every year.
example_sentences: Could you hold my bag for a moment?
The hall holds about four hundred people.
entry_json.avoid: Hold is irregular: hold, held, held.

entry_json.definition: an empty space in something, or a space that goes right through it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was a hole in the road that nobody repaired for a year.
example_sentences: I have a hole in my jacket pocket.
The rain came through a hole in the roof.

confusables.difference: Hole is a gap. Whole means complete: the whole day. They sound the same, so check your spelling.

entry_json.definition: a period of time when you do not work or study, often spent away from home
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I take my holiday in September because flights are cheaper then.
example_sentences: We went on holiday to the coast last summer.
Public holidays are set by the government.

confusables.difference: Holiday is British; vacation is American. British English says "on holiday", not "on vacation".

entry_json.avoid: We say "go on holiday" and "be on holiday", never "go to holiday".

entry_json.definition: the place where you live
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I work from home two days a week, which saves three hours of travel.
example_sentences: I usually get home at about seven.
More people now work from home than before.

confusables.difference: A house is the building. Home is where you live and feel you belong, which might be a flat or a room.

entry_json.avoid: Home takes no preposition after go: "go home", never "go to home".

entry_json.definition: school work that a teacher gives you to do at home
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We had two hours of homework every night, which left no time for sport.
example_sentences: Have you done your homework yet?
Some schools have stopped setting homework for young children.
entry_json.avoid: Homework is uncountable: "a lot of homework", never "homeworks" or "a homework". You DO homework, you do not make it.

entry_json.definition: to want something to happen and think it might
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I hope to start the course in September if my visa arrives in time.
example_sentences: I hope the weather improves before the weekend.
We hope that more people will use the service.

confusables.difference: Hope is for things that are still possible: I hope it rains. Wish is for things that are unlikely or untrue: I wish it rained more.

entry_json.avoid: After hope, use a present tense for the future: "I hope he comes", not "I hope he will come to come".

entry_json.definition: a large animal that people ride and that can pull heavy things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandfather used a horse on the farm long after tractors arrived.
example_sentences: She learned to ride a horse at seven.
Horses were the main form of transport for centuries.

entry_json.definition: a building where doctors and nurses look after people who are ill or hurt
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The nearest hospital is forty minutes away, which worries older residents.
example_sentences: He was taken to hospital after the accident.
Hospitals in rural areas struggle to recruit staff.
entry_json.avoid: British English drops the article when you are a patient: "in hospital". American English says "in the hospital".

entry_json.definition: having a high temperature
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It gets so hot in July that most people work early and rest at midday.
example_sentences: Be careful, the plate is hot.
Hot weather increases demand for electricity.

entry_json.definition: a building where you pay to sleep and eat when you are away from home
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The hotel was clean and cheap, and ten minutes from the exam centre.
example_sentences: We stayed in a small hotel near the beach.
New hotels have changed the character of the old town.

entry_json.definition: a period of sixty minutes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I spend an hour a day on vocabulary, split into two short sessions.
example_sentences: The journey takes about two hours.
Staff work a thirty-five hour week.
entry_json.avoid: The h is silent, so we write "an hour", not "a hour".

entry_json.definition: a building that people live in, usually with more than one floor
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Buying a house is out of reach for most people my age.
example_sentences: They live in a small house near the park.
House prices have doubled in a decade.

entry_json.definition: in what way, or to what degree
entry_json.own_context_sentence: How you revise matters more than how many hours you sit at the desk.
example_sentences: How did you get to work this morning?
How long have you lived here?

confusables.difference: "How is she?" asks about health. "What is she like?" asks about personality. Do not use how to ask for a description.

entry_json.definition: used to say something that is different from what was said before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Online courses are cheaper. However, many students find it hard to stay motivated.
example_sentences: The plan was popular. However, it was never funded.
There are, however, two serious objections.

confusables.difference: But joins two clauses inside one sentence. However usually starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma. "However I went" without the comma is wrong.

entry_json.avoid: Do not join two sentences with a comma before however. Use a full stop or a semicolon.

entry_json.definition: extremely large
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is a huge difference between reading English and using it under pressure.
example_sentences: The stadium is huge and rarely full.
Huge amounts of food are thrown away every day.

entry_json.definition: connected with people rather than animals or machines
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Human activity is the main cause of the rise in temperature.
example_sentences: Machines cannot replace human judgement entirely.
Human beings need about eight hours of sleep.

entry_json.definition: wanting to eat
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I get hungry mid-morning, so I keep fruit in my bag.
example_sentences: Are you hungry? There is soup in the kitchen.
Millions of children still go to school hungry.
entry_json.avoid: We say "I am hungry", not "I have hunger".

entry_json.definition: to cause pain to someone, or to feel pain
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My back hurts after a long day at a badly designed desk.
example_sentences: He hurt his knee playing football.
Nobody was seriously hurt in the crash.

confusables.difference: Hurt is the everyday word and can mean emotional pain too. Injure is more formal and physical, and is the better word in a written report.

entry_json.avoid: Hurt does not change: hurt, hurt, hurt.

entry_json.definition: the man that a woman or man is married to
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Her husband works abroad, so she manages the family alone most of the year.
example_sentences: My husband and I met at university.
Husbands now take a larger share of childcare.

entry_json.definition: water that has become hard because it is very cold
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was ice on the inside of the window that first winter.
example_sentences: Could I have a glass of water with ice?
Sea ice is melting faster than models predicted.

entry_json.definition: a thought or plan in your mind
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The idea that everyone should go to university is worth questioning.
example_sentences: That is a good idea.
I have no idea how long the process takes.
entry_json.avoid: We say "the idea THAT students should pay", not "the idea to students should pay".

entry_json.definition: the best possible; perfect for a purpose
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The flat was not ideal, but it was close to campus and I could afford it.
example_sentences: This is an ideal place to study quietly.
In an ideal world, public transport would be free.

entry_json.definition: to recognise something and say what or who it is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The first step is to identify which skill is holding your score down.
example_sentences: The study identifies three main causes.
Police were able to identify the driver.

entry_json.definition: used to talk about something that may happen or may be true
entry_json.own_context_sentence: If I had started reading earlier, my score would have been higher.
example_sentences: If it rains, we will move indoors.
Let me know if you need any help.
entry_json.avoid: After if, do not use will for the condition: "If it rains, I will stay", never "If it will rain".

entry_json.definition: not well; having a disease
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was ill for the whole of the first week and missed three lectures.
example_sentences: She has been seriously ill since March.
Employees who feel ill should stay at home.

confusables.difference: In British English, ill means unwell and sick often means about to vomit. American English uses sick for both. Say "I feel ill" in Britain.

entry_json.avoid: Ill goes after the verb: "she is ill". Before a noun, use "sick": "a sick child", not "an ill child".

entry_json.definition: the state of being unwell, or a particular period of being unwell
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A long illness kept her out of school for most of the year.
example_sentences: Mental illness affects one adult in four.
He returned to work after a short illness.

entry_json.definition: a picture, or the way people think about someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city has worked hard to change its image as an industrial town.
example_sentences: The report includes satellite images of the coast.
Social media shapes how young people see their own image.

entry_json.definition: to form a picture of something in your mind
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is hard to imagine life without a phone, though I managed until I was twenty.
example_sentences: Imagine you are explaining this to a child.
I cannot imagine living somewhere with no public transport.
entry_json.avoid: Imagine is followed by -ing, not to: "imagine living abroad", never "imagine to live abroad".

entry_json.definition: at once, with no waiting
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Reply immediately if the university asks for extra documents.
example_sentences: The alarm went off and everyone left immediately.
The effect was felt almost immediately.

entry_json.definition: having a big effect, or mattering a great deal
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is important to practise under exam conditions, not just to study.
example_sentences: Sleep is more important than an extra hour of revision.
This is the most important point in the whole report.
entry_json.avoid: Say "It is important to do X" or "It is important that X should be done". Not "It is important doing X".

entry_json.definition: not able to happen or be done
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is almost impossible to find a quiet room in that library after four.
example_sentences: Predicting the results with any accuracy is impossible.
Nothing is impossible if you have enough time.
entry_json.avoid: Impossible is already absolute, so avoid "very impossible". Say "almost impossible" or "completely impossible".

entry_json.definition: to become better, or to make something better
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My listening improved once I started watching the news every day.
example_sentences: The government wants to improve rural transport.
Air quality has improved slightly since 2015.
entry_json.avoid: Improve can stand alone: "my English improved". You do not need "improved itself".

entry_json.definition: inside something, or during a period of time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have lived in this city since 2019 and in this flat since last March.
example_sentences: The keys are in my bag.
The report will be published in June.

confusables.difference: In shows where something already is. Into shows movement from outside to inside: "He walked into the room" and then "He is in the room".

entry_json.avoid: Use in with months, years and seasons (in July, in 2020), on with days (on Monday), and at with times (at six).

entry_json.definition: to have something as one of its parts
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The fee includes all materials, which is why it looks expensive at first.
example_sentences: The price includes breakfast.
The survey included two thousand households.

confusables.difference: Include names some of the parts, and there may be others. Contain describes everything inside: "the box contains six eggs", "the fee includes insurance".

entry_json.definition: counted as part of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Service is included, so there is no need to leave a tip.
example_sentences: Breakfast is included in the room rate.
All taxes are included in the final price.

entry_json.definition: used to say that someone or something is part of the group being talked about
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Six countries, including Japan and Germany, showed the same pattern.
example_sentences: The course covers four skills, including writing.
Everyone including the manager had to reapply.
entry_json.avoid: Including introduces examples, so it is never followed by a full list. Use "consisting of" if you name every part.

entry_json.definition: to become larger in number or amount, or to make something larger
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The number of students living at home has increased sharply since 2010.
example_sentences: Sales increased by twelve per cent last year.
Cycling increases both fitness and concentration.

confusables.difference: In Task 1 both work, but increase can take an object ("increase taxes") while rise cannot. You cannot "rise taxes".

entry_json.avoid: The verb is stressed on the second syllable and the noun on the first: to inCREASE, an INcrease.

entry_json.definition: extremely good or surprising; hard to believe
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The view from the top was incredible after a three-hour climb.
example_sentences: She showed incredible patience with beginners.
The speed of change has been incredible.
entry_json.avoid: Incredible is informal when it means very good. In Task 2, prefer "remarkable" or "striking".

entry_json.definition: not controlled or supported by other people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Living alone made me far more independent than any course could have.
example_sentences: The study was carried out by an independent research group.
Children should be encouraged to become independent learners.
entry_json.avoid: Independent takes OF, not from: "independent of her parents".

entry_json.definition: one single person, considered separately from a group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Change depends on governments as much as on individuals.
example_sentences: Each individual learns at a different speed.
The rights of the individual must be protected.

entry_json.definition: the making of things in factories, or all the businesses of one type
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The tourist industry now employs more people here than farming does.
example_sentences: The car industry has been slow to change.
Heavy industry declined after the 1980s.

entry_json.definition: relaxed and friendly, like the language you use with friends, not the careful language of work or school
entry_json.own_context_sentence: An informal chat with my tutor helped more than three formal meetings.
example_sentences: The dress code is informal.
Informal language is fine in an email to a friend.
entry_json.avoid: Informal language, contractions and slang lose marks in Writing Task 2. Keep them for Speaking.

entry_json.definition: facts or details about someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The website gives clear information about visa requirements.
example_sentences: For further information, contact the admissions office.
Too much information can be as unhelpful as too little.
entry_json.avoid: Information is uncountable. Say "a piece of information" or "some information", never "an information" or "informations".

entry_json.definition: when part of a person's body is hurt in an accident or attack
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A knee injury ended his season and nearly ended his career.
example_sentences: She was treated for minor injuries.
Workplace injuries have fallen since the new rules.

entry_json.definition: a small animal with six legs, such as an ant or a fly
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Insect numbers have fallen sharply where pesticides are used heavily.
example_sentences: Bees are the most useful insects we have.
Insect bites are common in the wet season.

entry_json.definition: in or into a building, box or other space
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We waited inside the station because the rain would not stop.
example_sentences: There was nothing inside the box.
It is warmer inside than out.

confusables.difference: Inside is usually followed by a noun: inside the car. Indoors stands alone and means not outside: "stay indoors".

entry_json.definition: in the place of someone or something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I took the bus instead, because the train was cancelled again.
example_sentences: The meeting was cancelled, so we spoke on the phone instead.
Instead of driving, try cycling for a month.
entry_json.avoid: "Instead" ends a sentence; "instead of" comes before a noun or -ing: "instead of going", not "instead to go".

entry_json.definition: information telling you how to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Read the instructions on the front page before you start the test.
example_sentences: Follow the instructions carefully.
The instructions were printed in four languages.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to teach people how to do something, such as drive a car or swim
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My driving instructor was patient with a very nervous learner.
example_sentences: The swimming instructor works with beginners.
Fitness instructors must be qualified.

confusables.difference: An instructor teaches a practical skill such as driving or skiing. A teacher usually works in a school with academic subjects.

entry_json.definition: an object used for making music, or a tool used for careful work
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a musical instrument as a child improves concentration later.
example_sentences: She plays two instruments well.
The laboratory instruments are checked every month.

entry_json.definition: able to learn and understand things well
entry_json.own_context_sentence: He is intelligent, but he never learned how to revise.
example_sentences: Dolphins are highly intelligent animals.
Intelligent students still need good teaching.

confusables.difference: Intelligent describes real mental ability. Clever can suggest quickness or even trickery, and is more informal in British English.

entry_json.definition: the feeling of wanting to know about something; also the extra money you pay when you borrow money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My interest in languages started with subtitles, not with lessons.
example_sentences: There is growing interest in electric bikes.
The loan carries five per cent interest.
entry_json.avoid: You have an interest IN something, not "of" something.

entry_json.definition: wanting to know or learn more about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have always been interested in how cities are planned.
example_sentences: Are you interested in joining the study group?
Few students were interested in the topic at first.

confusables.difference: You are interested (that is how you feel). The thing is interesting (that is what it does). "I am interesting" claims that other people find you fascinating.

entry_json.definition: making you want to know more; not boring
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The most interesting part of the course was the fieldwork.
example_sentences: That is an interesting point.
The article raises several interesting questions.

entry_json.definition: involving two or more countries
entry_json.own_context_sentence: International students pay roughly three times the local fee.
example_sentences: The airport handles both domestic and international flights.
Climate change requires international cooperation.

entry_json.definition: the system that connects computers around the world
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Slow internet at home is the main reason I study at the library.
example_sentences: I found the course on the internet.
Access to the internet is now considered a basic service.
entry_json.avoid: We say "on the internet", with the. Never "in internet".

entry_json.definition: a formal meeting where someone is asked questions, for a job or research
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I had three interviews before I was offered anything at all.
example_sentences: The job interview lasted forty minutes.
The researchers conducted interviews with fifty families.

entry_json.definition: moving to the inside of a place or thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She walked into the exam room two minutes before it started.
example_sentences: Put the shopping into the fridge.
The river flows into the sea just south of the town.

entry_json.definition: to tell people someone's name when they meet; also to bring in something new
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Let me introduce myself: I am here about the accommodation.
example_sentences: She introduced me to her colleagues.
The government introduced a new tax on plastic bags.
entry_json.avoid: You introduce someone TO someone else. "Introduce me your friend" is wrong.

entry_json.definition: the first part of a piece of writing or a talk, which says what it is about
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My introduction is now three sentences, and my score went up.
example_sentences: The introduction should restate the question in your own words.
The introduction of the new system caused some confusion.

entry_json.definition: to make or design something that did not exist before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Whoever invented the bicycle solved a problem cities still have.
example_sentences: The telephone was invented in the nineteenth century.
She invented a simple device for testing water.

entry_json.definition: a thing that someone has made for the first time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The washing machine may be the invention that changed daily life most.
example_sentences: Printing was one of the most important inventions in history.
The invention of the internet changed how we work.

entry_json.definition: a message asking someone to come to an event or join you
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I turned down the invitation because the exam was two days later.
example_sentences: Thank you for the invitation to the conference.
Invitations were sent out a month in advance.

entry_json.definition: to ask someone to come to an event or to do something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My neighbours invited me to dinner in my first week, which I never forgot.
example_sentences: We invited about thirty people to the wedding.
She was invited to speak at the conference.
entry_json.avoid: Invite someone TO a place or event: "invite her to the party", not "invite her at the party".

entry_json.definition: to include something as a necessary part; to affect or include someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The job involves travelling to three sites every week.
example_sentences: The process involves several stages.
Parents should be involved in the decision.
entry_json.avoid: Involve is followed by -ing, not to: "the job involves working nights".

entry_json.definition: a piece of land with water all around it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I grew up on a small island where everybody knew everybody.
example_sentences: The island can only be reached by boat.
Low-lying islands are most at risk from rising seas.
entry_json.avoid: The s is silent: it sounds like EYE-land.

entry_json.definition: the thing or animal already mentioned; also used for weather and time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It takes about half an hour to walk, and it is quicker than the bus.
example_sentences: It is raining again.
The report is long, but it is worth reading.
entry_json.avoid: English sentences need a subject: "It is cold today", never "Is cold today".

entry_json.definition: one single thing in a list or group
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every item on the packing list mattered, and I still forgot my adapter.
example_sentences: Please tick each item as you check it.
The most expensive item was the flight.

entry_json.definition: belonging to the thing or animal already mentioned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The city has changed its transport policy three times in five years.
example_sentences: The company published its results yesterday.
The dog wagged its tail.

confusables.difference: Its shows possession: the company and its staff. It's is short for it is or it has. If you can say "it is", write it's; otherwise write its.

entry_json.avoid: Never write "it's" when you mean belonging to. This is the single most common apostrophe error in English.

entry_json.definition: used when the same thing or animal is both the subject and the object
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The problem will not solve itself, whatever the minister says.
example_sentences: The building itself is fine; the location is the problem.
The machine switches itself off after ten minutes.

entry_json.definition: a short coat that covers the top half of the body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I wore the same jacket every day of that first winter.
example_sentences: Take a jacket; it gets cold in the evening.
He wore a suit jacket to the interview.

entry_json.definition: a sweet food made from fruit and sugar that you put on bread
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My grandmother made jam every August from the fruit in the garden.
example_sentences: I had toast and jam for breakfast.
The shop sells homemade strawberry jam.

confusables.difference: Jam also means a line of cars that cannot move: a traffic jam. Context makes the meaning clear, but never say "a jam of cars".

entry_json.definition: a kind of music with a strong beat, in which players often make up the music as they play
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I discovered jazz through a radio programme I could not sleep through.
example_sentences: The bar has live jazz on Thursdays.
Jazz began in the United States in the early twentieth century.

entry_json.definition: strong trousers, usually blue, that people wear every day
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I wore jeans to the interview and realised at the door it was a mistake.
example_sentences: These jeans are too tight now.
Jeans are acceptable in most offices these days.
entry_json.avoid: Jeans is always plural: "my jeans are", not "my jeans is". Say "a pair of jeans" for one item.

entry_json.definition: rings, necklaces and other decorative objects worn on the body
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She wears almost no jewellery apart from a watch her father gave her.
example_sentences: The jewellery was kept in a small wooden box.
Gold jewellery is a traditional wedding gift in my country.
entry_json.avoid: Jewellery is uncountable, and British English spells it with two l's. Say "a piece of jewellery", not "a jewellery".

entry_json.definition: the work that someone does to earn money
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My first job paid badly but taught me how an office actually works.
example_sentences: She got a job in a research laboratory.
Automation may remove millions of jobs.

confusables.difference: Job is countable and means a particular position: "I have two jobs". Work is uncountable and means activity: "I have a lot of work". Not "a work".

entry_json.definition: to become a member of a group; to connect two things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I joined a conversation club, and my confidence changed within a month.
example_sentences: He joined the company in 2019.
A short bridge joins the two halves of the town.
entry_json.avoid: You join a club with no preposition: "join the gym", not "join to the gym".

entry_json.definition: something you say or do to make people laugh
entry_json.own_context_sentence: His jokes did not translate, which taught me how local humour is.
example_sentences: She told a joke that nobody understood.
It started as a joke and became a real business.
entry_json.avoid: In English you TELL a joke; you do not "say a joke".

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to write news reports or make news programmes
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A journalist visited the school and wrote about our reading project.
example_sentences: She works as a journalist for a national newspaper.
Journalists face real danger in some countries.

entry_json.definition: an act of travelling from one place to another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My daily journey takes an hour each way, which I use for listening practice.
example_sentences: The journey by train takes three hours.
Long journeys to work make people less healthy.

confusables.difference: A journey is the travelling itself. A trip includes going somewhere and coming back, usually for a purpose: a business trip made up of two journeys.
Travel is uncountable and general: "travel broadens the mind". Journey is one countable act. Not "I made a travel".

entry_json.definition: a drink that comes out of fruit or vegetables
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A glass of orange juice costs more than the oranges it comes from.
example_sentences: Would you like some apple juice?
Fruit juice contains as much sugar as many soft drinks.

entry_json.definition: to push yourself off the ground into the air
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Prices jumped by nearly a fifth in a single year.
example_sentences: The children jumped over the wall.
He jumped up when the phone rang.

entry_json.definition: only; or a very short time ago
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I have just finished the practice test and I am too tired to check it.
example_sentences: It costs just two pounds.
She had just left when you called.
entry_json.avoid: With the present perfect, just goes between have and the past participle: "I have just eaten".

entry_json.definition: to continue to have something; or to continue doing something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I keep a notebook of new words and review it every Sunday.
example_sentences: Keep the receipt in case there is a problem.
Prices keep rising despite the promises.
entry_json.avoid: Keep is followed by -ing for repeated actions: "he keeps asking", never "he keeps to ask". Keep is irregular: keep, kept, kept.

entry_json.definition: a small metal object for opening a lock; also the most important thing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Practice is the key to fluency, and there is no way around it.
example_sentences: I locked myself out because I left the key inside.
Communication is the key to good teamwork.

entry_json.definition: a child
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The kids in my street play football until it is completely dark.
example_sentences: We took the kids to the park.
When I was a kid, we had no television at all.
entry_json.avoid: Kid is informal. In Writing Task 2 use "child" or "children".

entry_json.definition: to make a person, animal or plant die
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Air pollution kills more people each year than road accidents do.
example_sentences: The frost killed most of the young plants.
Malaria still kills hundreds of thousands of people.

entry_json.definition: one thousand metres; we use it to say how far one place is from another
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I cycle about eight kilometres a day, mostly to and from work.
example_sentences: The beach is two kilometres from the hotel.
The new road is thirty kilometres long.
entry_json.avoid: British spelling is kilometre; American is kilometer. The short form is km with no full stop.

entry_json.definition: a man who rules a country because of his family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The king has no real political power, but he opens parliament each year.
example_sentences: The king ruled for over fifty years.
Kings and queens appear throughout the country's history.

entry_json.definition: the room where food is prepared and cooked
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Six of us shared one kitchen, which is how I learned to plan meals.
example_sentences: The flat has a small kitchen and one bathroom.
Restaurant kitchens are inspected twice a year.

entry_json.definition: the part in the middle of your leg that moves when you sit down or go up stairs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A knee injury stopped me running for almost a year.
example_sentences: He fell and hurt his knee.
Cycling puts less strain on the knees than running.
entry_json.avoid: The k is silent: knee sounds like "nee".

entry_json.definition: a tool that you hold and use to cut food and other things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, which surprised me.
example_sentences: Use a knife and fork, not your fingers.
The knife was too blunt to cut the bread.
entry_json.avoid: The k is silent, and the plural is knives, not knifes.

entry_json.definition: to hit a door with your hand to let people know you are there
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Someone knocked on the door in the middle of the listening test.
example_sentences: Please knock before entering.
She knocked twice and then let herself in.
entry_json.avoid: The k is silent. You knock ON a door, not "knock the door", unless you mean hit it hard.

entry_json.definition: to have information about something, or to have met someone before
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I know the theory well, but I still panic when the timer starts.
example_sentences: Do you know how long the visa takes?
I have known her since primary school.

confusables.difference: Know is a state: you already have the information. Find out is an action: you get information you did not have. "I want to find out", not "I want to know" when you mean to discover.

entry_json.avoid: Know is not used in the continuous: "I know", never "I am knowing". It is irregular: know, knew, known.

entry_json.definition: the facts and understanding that a person has
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My knowledge of grammar was good; my ability to use it was not.
example_sentences: The job requires a good knowledge of statistics.
Knowledge of a second language is an advantage.
entry_json.avoid: Knowledge is uncountable: "much knowledge", never "knowledges". You have knowledge OF a subject.

entry_json.definition: a room where scientists do their work and tests
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We spent two afternoons a week in the lab, which is where I learned most.
example_sentences: The samples are being tested in the lab.
The university built a new language lab.

confusables.difference: Lab is the short, everyday form. Laboratory is the full word and is better in formal writing.

entry_json.definition: a polite word for a woman
entry_json.own_context_sentence: An older lady on the bus explained the route to me in careful English.
example_sentences: Ladies and gentlemen, please take your seats.
The lady at the desk was very helpful.

confusables.difference: Woman is the neutral word and the right one in writing. Lady is polite in speech but can sound old-fashioned. Use woman in Task 2.

entry_json.definition: a large area of water with land all around it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The lake freezes in January and half the town walks on it.
example_sentences: We swam in the lake every morning.
The lake has shrunk by a third since 1990.

entry_json.definition: an object that gives light
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A small desk lamp made late-night study far easier on my eyes.
example_sentences: Switch the lamp on; it is getting dark.
Street lamps now use LED bulbs.

entry_json.definition: the dry part of the earth that we live on, not the sea
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Land near the city is too expensive for young farmers to buy.
example_sentences: The farm covers sixty hectares of land.
Much of the land is used for grazing.
entry_json.avoid: Land is uncountable in this sense: "a piece of land", not "a land". "A land" means a country and sounds poetic.

entry_json.definition: the system of words that people of one country or group use to communicate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Learning a second language changed how I hear my own.
example_sentences: English is the main language of scientific research.
Hundreds of languages disappear every century.
entry_json.avoid: Language names take a capital letter: English, Arabic, Japanese.

entry_json.definition: a small computer you can carry and use anywhere
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My laptop is six years old and still fast enough for everything I do.
example_sentences: I take my laptop to the library every day.
Students are expected to bring their own laptops.

entry_json.definition: big in size or amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A large part of my income goes on rent alone.
example_sentences: The company employs a large number of part-time staff.
We booked a large room for the workshop.

confusables.difference: Large and big both mean not small, but large is slightly more formal and is preferred with numbers and amounts: "a large number", not "a big number", in writing.

entry_json.definition: arriving or happening after the expected time
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was late for my own interview because the train stopped for an hour.
example_sentences: The bus was twenty minutes late.
Late payments carry a small charge.

confusables.difference: Late means after the expected time. Lately means recently: "I have been busy lately". They are not related in meaning.

entry_json.avoid: You are late FOR something: "late for class", not "late to class" in British English.

entry_json.definition: at a time after now or after the time mentioned
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I will look at the results later, when I can think clearly.
example_sentences: Two years later, she was running the department.
See you later.

entry_json.definition: to make sounds that show you think something is funny
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The whole class laughed, and suddenly the lesson felt easier.
example_sentences: He laughed at his own mistake.
It is healthy to laugh at yourself occasionally.
entry_json.avoid: You laugh AT something. "Laugh with someone" is friendly; "laugh at someone" can be unkind.

entry_json.definition: the sound of people laughing
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There was laughter from the next room all through the exam briefing.
example_sentences: The talk was interrupted by laughter.
Laughter is said to reduce stress.
entry_json.avoid: Laughter is uncountable: "a lot of laughter", never "laughters".

entry_json.definition: a rule made by a government that everyone must follow
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The law changed in 2019, and cycling helmets became compulsory.
example_sentences: It is against the law to drive without insurance.
The government passed a new law on plastic waste.
entry_json.avoid: Say "against the law" or "break the law". "Do a law" is not English.

entry_json.definition: a person whose job is to help people with the law and speak for them
entry_json.own_context_sentence: We needed a lawyer for the contract, and it cost more than the deposit.
example_sentences: She trained as a lawyer before moving into teaching.
Lawyers are expensive in every country I know of.

entry_json.definition: not wanting to work or try hard
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I was not lazy, I simply had no idea how to study effectively.
example_sentences: It is easy to get lazy during a long holiday.
Calling students lazy usually hides a teaching problem.
entry_json.avoid: Lazy is a criticism. Do not use it about a person in a formal essay unless you can support it.

entry_json.definition: the person who is the head of a group, company or country
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A good team leader listens more than she speaks.
example_sentences: World leaders met to discuss the crisis.
She became the leader of the project after six months.

entry_json.definition: to get knowledge or a skill by studying or practising
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I learned more English in six months of work than in six years of school.
example_sentences: Children learn languages very quickly.
I am learning to drive at the moment.

confusables.difference: Learn is the result: you now know it. Study is the activity: you sit down and work at it. You can study for hours and learn nothing.
You learn something yourself. You teach it to someone else. "She learned me English" is wrong; use taught.

entry_json.definition: the process of getting knowledge or skills
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Online learning suits me because I can repeat the difficult parts.
example_sentences: Learning a language takes years, not weeks.
The school promotes independent learning.

entry_json.definition: to go away from a place; also to let something stay where it is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I leave the house at half past seven to avoid the worst of the traffic.
example_sentences: She left the company last year.
I left my umbrella on the train again.

confusables.difference: You leave an object somewhere; you forget a fact. "I left my keys at home", not "I forgot my keys at home".

entry_json.avoid: Leave is irregular: leave, left, left. "Leave for London" means head towards it; "leave London" means go away from it.

entry_json.definition: a talk given to a group of students on a subject
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The lecture was recorded, so I watched it twice at half speed.
example_sentences: The lecture starts at nine in the main hall.
Attendance at lectures is no longer compulsory.

confusables.difference: A lecture is a long talk to a large group, usually at university. A lesson is a shorter class where the teacher works with you. Schools have lessons; universities have lectures.

entry_json.definition: on the side of the body where the heart is
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Take the second left turn and the entrance is on your left.
example_sentences: He writes with his left hand.
The chart on the left shows the figures for 2010.
entry_json.avoid: "Left" is also the past of leave. Context decides: "she left" is the verb; "the left side" is direction.

entry_json.definition: one of the long parts of the body that you stand and walk on
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My legs ached for two days after the climb.
example_sentences: He broke his leg playing rugby.
The table has one short leg and wobbles.

entry_json.definition: a yellow fruit with a sour taste
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I drink hot water with lemon every morning out of habit rather than belief.
example_sentences: Add a slice of lemon to the water.
Lemons grow well in the south of the country.

entry_json.definition: to give something to someone for a short time, expecting it back
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A classmate lent me her notes for the whole term, and I still owe her.
example_sentences: Could you lend me ten pounds until Friday?
Banks are lending less to small businesses.

confusables.difference: You LEND something to someone (it goes away from you). You BORROW something from someone (it comes towards you). "Can you borrow me a pen?" is wrong; say "Can you lend me a pen?"

entry_json.avoid: Lend is irregular: lend, lent, lent. Never "lended".
